editorials.heading: Why it matters
editorials.title: A weekend of new No. 1s
paras: Zverev (the season's rankings race), Rybakina (WTA world No. 1) and Antonelli (a commanding Formula 1 lead) all took a career-defining step in the same few days. Across three unrelated sports, 2026 is settling into a season that crowns fresh names at the very top rather than the familiar incumbents.

A strong Swiss weekend, on and off the podium. Werro's world title is the headline, but the domestic game supplied its own story: Xherdan Shaqiri, at the veteran end of his career, single-handedly dragging FC Basel out of a crisis under a coach three days into the job. Different scales, same theme — Swiss sport had a good week.

editorials.heading: Cross-cutting threads
paras: 1. The verification gap is now the binding constraint on reinforcement learning — and half the field is racing to close it. The single clearest theme across this week's ML papers is that the recent reasoning gains from reinforcement learning (RL — training a model by rewarding good outcomes rather than imitating examples) came almost entirely from domains with a cheap, trustworthy answer-checker: a maths answer key, a unit test. Take that checker away and progress stalls. "Proof-Carrying Cognition" states this most sharply — it proves that past a certain point, throwing more inference compute at an unsound reward makes a model look better while getting worse — but the same worry drives three otherwise-unrelated papers. TRACE manufactures a trustworthy reward by hiding the answer inside a simulator; T1 leans on the one checker that is always sound (does the code actually run and pass its tests?); and "Do Agents Know When They Succeed?" gives up on external checking entirely and reads the model's own internal activations for a success signal. The analytical plane bears this out: "reinforcement learning" recurred as a cross-stream entity four times this window (ai-ml and weekend), and the reward problem is what ties the cluster together. The uncomfortable implication for anyone reading benchmark press releases: outside maths and code, a headline RL number is only as trustworthy as the verifier behind it, and this week gives you the tools to ask how sound that is.

2. AI became a genuine mathematical instrument this week — and the same week reminded us what mathematics is actually for. The loudest science story of the week is a claimed finite-time singularity in fluid equations, produced with heavy AI assistance and checked in the Lean proof assistant (see below). But read alongside two quieter Quanta pieces — a rare new human proof of the four-color theorem, and a panel at the International Congress of Mathematicians asking "what is math for in the age of AI?" — a more honest picture emerges than "AI solved a Millennium problem." The decisive strategy behind the fluid results came from two human mathematicians (Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa) working by hand; the machines executed and formalised it. Terence Tao, who has watched this closely, put the counterweight plainly: "the actual solving of these problems is only a proxy goal for the primary goal of developing mathematical understanding and insight." The four-color theorem — solved by computer in the 1970s, yet still drawing mathematicians back for a proof that explains — is the same lesson from the other direction. What machines are getting good at (producing and verifying answers) and what mathematicians actually want (insight) are pulling apart, and this week you could watch both happen at once.

3. The efficiency frontier is finally getting a "why," not just a "how." For two years, making large models cheaper to run has been a bag of empirical tricks that happen to work. This week three papers replaced folklore with mechanism. "Why Does Post-Training Quantization Work?" explains why squashing weights to 4-bit barely dents accuracy — layer-to-layer errors partly cancel, and the output geometry protects the model's most confident predictions. "Don't Drop Dropout" resurrects a training technique the field abandoned on hearsay and shows, across 2,400 experiments, that it lowers loss when tuned. FlexComp turns context-compression ratio from a fixed deployment decision into a per-request knob. The common thread — and the reason it matters to a reader who runs models locally or pays a serving bill — is that the pressure driving all of it is the cost of long-context reasoning agents: the KV cache (the per-token memory a model accumulates as it thinks) is the bottleneck, and it is the explicit design target of the week's headline open-weight release, DeepSeek V4.1-Flash, too. Understanding why the cheap tricks work is what tells you where they will break.

stories.headline: RL for LLMs wastes compute on easy problems
stories.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL — training a model by rewarding correct answers) improves an LLM far more on problems it can already usually solve than on genuinely hard ones — a pattern the authors name the "Matthew effect" (the rich get richer). They argue standard RL squanders compute re-solving easy problems, and introduce Never Give Up (NGU): keep sampling a problem until a correct answer appears, then, using asynchronous RL, spend fewer samples on the easy problems and pour the freed budget into the hard ones.
stories.why: Frontier RL runs are enormously expensive, and this reframes part of that spend as misallocated rather than merely insufficient — a scheduling change, not more GPUs, closes some of the hard-problem gap.

stories.headline: Fully open 7B model leans on tools not memorization
stories.summary: ZGCM-1 is a 7-billion-parameter dense model trained from scratch with a fully open recipe, on the premise that a small model cannot memorize the open web but can compensate by pairing internal reasoning with external tool use (search, code) over a 256K-token context. The recipe combines an interleaved sliding-window/full-attention design, an FP8 Muon optimizer, and a staged curriculum that scales context from 16K to 256K and recasts tool-interaction traces as Markov decision processes (a formalism for sequential decisions) during mid-training.
stories.why: Open, reproducible recipes for capable small models are scarce — most frontier work is closed — so a from-scratch, documented 7B aimed at math and agentic search lowers the barrier to study and build on. The paper is bylined to an unnamed "ZGCM Team" and the efficiency claims are the authors' own; treat them as unverified until independently reproduced.

stories.headline: Reasoning models fail logical twins of solved tasks
stories.summary: "Systematicity" is the principle that understanding a concept implies understanding close variations of it. The authors take rule-induction tasks from cognitive science and build structurally equivalent variants — the same underlying rule, recombined or with symbols substituted — then check whether a model that solves one variant also solves its isomorphs. Often it does not: models fail variants that are logically identical to problems they just got right.
stories.why: It is direct evidence that apparent reasoning can be brittle and non-compositional — getting a benchmark item right does not mean the model has grasped the rule behind it, which bears on any use that assumes it will generalize.

stories.headline: Cheaper training-data attribution at model scale
stories.summary: Data attribution measures how much each training example shaped a given prediction — the basis for data valuation, machine unlearning (removing a datapoint's influence after the fact), and interpretability. Exact "metagradient" methods such as MAGIC differentiate through the whole training run but need a separate run per prediction, which is prohibitive. This work recasts budgeted attribution as estimating a large "influence matrix" from a small number of measurements, and shows which measurements best recover it.
stories.why: If influence can be approximated from a few measurements instead of one run per query, attribution becomes tractable at model scale — practical for unlearning requests, copyright and data-valuation disputes, and debugging which data drove a behavior. (MAGIC co-author Andrew Ilyas is on the paper.)

stories.headline: Microsoft publishes Humanist AI Code of Conduct
stories.summary: Microsoft publishes a "Humanist AI Code of Conduct". Microsoft AI released a code of conduct staking out an explicit position in the AI-welfare debate: per the document and secondary coverage, it calls for models whose "thinking" is legible to people, states that AI systems have no inner life, and rules out AI rights. It is a values statement rather than a product or policy change, but a notable public stance from a frontier lab as questions of model "welfare" gain attention.

stories.headline: Anthropic reportedly eyes a Nasdaq listing
stories.summary: The FT reports Anthropic is weighing a Nasdaq listing. The Financial Times reported that Anthropic is eyeing a Nasdaq listing and, per the report, is pointing to a claimed second profitable quarter to court investors ahead of a possible large IPO. This is reporting, not an Anthropic announcement, and the underlying financials are attributed to sources rather than confirmed filings — treat it as a signal of intent, not a done deal.

stories.headline: Diagnosing agent failures as a search problem
stories.summary: Long-horizon AI agents produce huge execution logs, and the true cause of a failure is often a single early action far from where things visibly broke. Existing root-cause methods hand an LLM the whole trace and ask for a one-shot verdict, which degrades as traces grow and relevant clues become sparse and scattered. The authors reframe diagnosis as a search problem — continually searching the trace for the responsible step rather than committing to an early guess.
stories.why: Reliable agents need to turn "it failed" into "it failed here, because of this", and one-shot judging does not scale to long traces; treating attribution as search is a route to debugging that holds up as agents run longer.

stories.headline: When an interrupted agent can safely resume
stories.summary: Agents get interrupted mid-task; restarting repeats completed work, but blindly continuing from a saved state can carry forward unverified or stale progress. The paper introduces "recoverability" as an explicit system primitive: a saved state is paired with a permitted recovery action and a contract binding that choice to supporting evidence and independent checks, so resuming is a deliberate decision rather than an automatic one. Their challenge set shows accurate-looking restoration can quietly hide disallowed reuse.
stories.why: As agents run longer and touch real files and tools, "resume from checkpoint" becomes a correctness question, not just a convenience — this frames the safeguards a runtime needs before it trusts its own saved state.

stories.headline: A DSL compiling attention variants to fused GPU kernels
stories.summary: Attention dominates transformer compute, and every new attention variant normally needs hand-written GPU code to run at usable speed. PyTorch's flex_attention lets researchers describe custom attention in Python but only handles changes applied after the core matrix multiply — which excludes RoPE (rotary position embedding, the positional scheme used by every major LLM), because RoPE acts before it. AttnFuse is a domain-specific language that makes such pre-multiplication transforms first-class, composing ten high-level building blocks into fused kernels.
stories.why: Lowering the cost of turning a new attention idea into production-speed code shortens the loop between architecture research and usable models — and it targets exactly the gap (RoPE) that existing tooling left open.

stories.headline: Bilaterals III reaches parliament floor
stories.summary: Switzerland's autumn parliamentary session opened on Monday 14 September, and the Council of States (the smaller chamber, which represents the cantons) is set to hold the first-ever floor debate on the Bilaterals III package — the roughly 2,000-page treaty deal renewing Switzerland's relationship with the EU. The chamber has reserved three session days for it and must decide, among other things, whether to place the package under a mandatory referendum, which would require a double majority of both voters and cantons to pass before it could take effect (an optional referendum would need only a majority of voters). The three-week session, which runs to 2 October, also queues up several other contested files: a proposed "armament fund" bankrolled by a temporary VAT rise — the Federal Council wants 0.5 percentage points for 12 years, while the Council of States' security committee counters with 0.2 points spread over 18 years — a watered-down "Lex UBS" over how much hard capital the bank must hold against its foreign subsidiaries after the Credit Suisse collapse, a 517-million-franc farm-support compromise meant to salvage the Mercosur free-trade agreement the National Council rejected in the summer session, and a revision of the Epidemics Act that would give the federal government standing authority to order nationwide measures such as a transport mask mandate.
stories.why: the Bilaterals III vote is the defining question for how Switzerland trades with and moves within its largest partner for a generation, and the referendum-type decision taken now shapes how high the bar will be at the ballot box. (Schweizer Parlament, Herbstsession 2026 ; SRF, 14.09.2026)

stories.headline: Werro takes inaugural Ultimate 800m title
stories.summary: Switzerland's Audrey Werro won the women's 800m at the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest on Saturday 12 September, finishing in 1:55.88 ahead of Britain's Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson (1:56.26) and the Netherlands' Femke Broeders-Bol. The Ultimate Championship is a new season-ending event — a three-day, invitation-only meet for the year's top-ranked athletes, with a $150,000 first prize in each discipline — and Werro's win confirmed what the whole summer had signalled: she is the world's best 800m runner. She had already beaten Hodgkinson repeatedly this season, winning in Stockholm, Paris and Zurich in under 1 minute 54 seconds, with a personal best of 1:53.70 that sits close to world-record territory. For a reader who does not follow athletics: the 800m — two laps of the track — is one of the sport's marquee middle-distance events, and Hodgkinson, a world indoor record-holder and Olympic champion, had been its dominant figure, so a Swiss athlete now beating her routinely is a genuine changing of the guard.
stories.why: Switzerland rarely produces a world-beating middle-distance runner, and Werro has become one inside a single season; this title — the first ever awarded in a brand-new championship — makes her the clear favourite heading into 2027.

stories.headline: Sweden's left bloc edges ahead
stories.summary: Sweden's centre-left opposition edged ahead in a knife-edge general election held on Sunday 13 September, with preliminary counts giving the four-party bloc led by former prime minister Magdalena Andersson a razor-thin seat lead over the sitting right-wing government — an outcome that, if it holds, would keep the far-right Sweden Democrats out of power. With counting still under way on Monday morning, the Social Democrats were the largest single party on roughly 27.6%, ahead of Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's Moderates around 20%, while the Sweden Democrats slipped back from the record score that made them the second-largest party in 2022. The result was still too close to formally call, and the final seat balance — reported at a margin of only a few seats — could shift as remaining and postal ballots are tallied.
stories.why: a bloc flip would end the arrangement under which Kristersson's minority government has governed with Sweden Democrat support, and would be one of the few recent European elections to check rather than extend the hard right's advance. (Euronews, 13.09.2026; Le Monde, 14.09.2026)

stories.headline: Russia strikes train near Polish border
stories.summary: A Russian strike hit a Warsaw-bound passenger train at the Yahodyn railway checkpoint on the Ukraine–Poland border on Sunday 13 September, shortly after a separate train carrying former British prime minister Boris Johnson and other European officials had passed through, prompting Poland and Ukraine to condemn the attack as an "escalation". Ukraine's rail operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, said Johnson and former CIA director David Petraeus had been in Kyiv for the Yalta European Strategy forum and were travelling on two separate trains around the time of the strike; it suggested the intended target may have been the diplomatic train, which had left ahead of schedule because of the threat of attack. Petraeus told the New York Times he heard drones overhead followed by an explosion, after which passengers were evacuated; no casualties were reported.
stories.why: a strike this close to the frontier of a NATO member, apparently near a train carrying Western political figures, sharpens the risk of the war spilling directly onto alliance territory. (RTÉ, 14.09.2026 )

stories.headline: Finland joins French deterrence plan
stories.summary: Finland said on Monday 14 September that it will join France's "forward deterrence" initiative, a bilateral framework that opens the door to joint exercises, dialogue on French nuclear doctrine, and the temporary deployment of French strategic air forces on Finnish soil. In a statement, the Finnish defence ministry stressed that the arrangement deepens defence cooperation but stops short of extending a French nuclear umbrella over the country. The initiative — France's offer to share elements of its independent deterrent with European partners in response to a more hostile Russia — was launched by President Emmanuel Macron in early 2026 and had drawn in eight countries plus Norway before Finland's decision.
stories.why: it is another sign of European states hedging against uncertainty over the US security guarantee by building a France-anchored deterrence layer, and Finland, which shares a long border with Russia, is a pointed addition. (defence-industry.eu, 14.09.2026 ; Le Monde, 14.09.2026)

stories.headline: Refs admit error on derby-winning goal
stories.summary: Manchester City beat Manchester United 1-0 at Old Trafford on Sunday 13 September, and the only goal — an Erling Haaland finish — has been disowned by the people who allowed it to stand. Pro Ref, the body that runs Premier League refereeing, admitted an "error of judgement" in awarding it, an unusually blunt public concession about a call that decided a derby. City won despite having Phil Foden sent off, so they saw out the closing stretch a man down. For a non-follower: the Manchester derby is English football's most-watched club rivalry, and VAR — the video review system meant to catch exactly this kind of mistake — did not overturn the goal, which is why an official mea culpa lands harder than the usual grumble about a referee.
stories.why: When the officials' own body concedes that the goal deciding the biggest domestic derby should not have counted, it sharpens the running complaint that video review has dented trust in the big calls rather than settling them.

stories.headline: Basel win at Luzern after Lichtsteiner exit
stories.summary: FC Basel won 4-2 away at Luzern in round 8, three days after sacking coach Stephan Lichtsteiner — the former Switzerland and Juventus full-back — on Wednesday 9 September following a run without a win. Under interim coach Luigi Nocentini, captain Xherdan Shaqiri ran the game with two goals and an assist (including a solo run for the fourth) to turn the match around after a poor start. In the same round, Servette beat Lausanne 1-0 in the Léman derby, played in front of closed supporter sections after crowd-trouble sanctions. Eight rounds in, Lugano lead the table on 19 points (from 7 games), Young Boys are second on 16, and Basel sit fourth on 13; Lausanne are bottom.
stories.why: A mid-week coaching change followed at once by an away win is a snapshot of an unsettled Swiss season — Lugano, not the traditional heavyweights, set the pace, and even a club Basel's size runs out of patience fast.

stories.headline: Antonelli wins Madrid, stretches title lead
stories.summary: Kimi Antonelli won the Madrid Grand Prix on Sunday 13 September, his eighth win of the season and a second in the space of a week after Monza. A late virtual safety car — a slow-down phase that neutralises the field after an incident — fell at the wrong moment for Lando Norris, costing the McLaren driver what had looked like a winning position and helping Antonelli through. The young Mercedes driver now leads the drivers' championship with 292 points, 81 clear of team-mate George Russell (211); Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton is third on 191 and Norris fourth on 186, and Mercedes hold both of the top two places. For context: F1's title is decided on points accumulated across the season, so a lead this size with roughly a third of the calendar left is close to decisive rather than merely healthy.
stories.why: Antonelli, in only his second full season, is not just winning but running away with it — the sport is watching a new outright favourite emerge while the established names (Verstappen, Norris, Hamilton) chase.

stories.headline: Zverev and Rybakina win US Open titles
stories.summary: Alexander Zverev beat American Ben Shelton 6-3, 7-6 (7-2), 5-7, 6-2 in the US Open men's final on Sunday 13 September — the second Grand Slam title of his career and the win that lifts him to No. 1 in the season's rankings race (the year-to-date standings, as opposed to the rolling 52-week ranking). Zverev, long cast as the best player yet to dominate a major, sealed his 53rd match win of a season in which he has been the tour's most consistent presence. A day earlier, Elena Rybakina beat Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 to win her first US Open, a result that also takes her to WTA world No. 1 for the first time. For the casual reader: the US Open is the last of tennis's four Grand Slams — the sport's four biggest tournaments — so these were the season's final marquee titles, and both finals doubled as rankings deciders.
stories.why: Two of the year's last big titles produced two new figures at the top — a men's champion who had carried a "nearly man" label for years, and a first-time women's No. 1.

stories.headline: Mas wins first Grand Tour as Pogačar crashes
stories.summary: The 2026 Vuelta a España, which opened on 23 August, ended with its 21st stage in Granada and Spain's Enric Mas (Movistar) as the overall winner — the first Grand Tour victory of his career. Mas had spent years as a podium regular without ever winning one of cycling's three-week races; he inherited the leader's red jersey when pre-race favourite Tadej Pogačar, who had already won three of the first six stages, crashed on stage 8 and abandoned injured. Mas won stage 9 and defended the lead to the finish, with Felix Gall and Richard Carapaz completing the podium. For context: the Vuelta is one of cycling's three Grand Tours (alongside the Tour de France and the Giro d'Italia), and Pogačar is the sport's dominant rider, so his exit reshaped the whole race.
stories.why: A first Grand Tour for a rider long written off as a perennial runner-up — handed the opening by the favourite's misfortune, then good enough to keep it — is a reminder that three-week races reward survival as much as brilliance.

stories.headline: Slavery complaint filed against three cantons
stories.summary: A US activist has filed a criminal complaint with Switzerland's Office of the Attorney General against the cantons of Zurich, Bern and Solothurn over their historical involvement in transatlantic slavery, though legal experts say a prosecution is all but hopeless. Shelley Moorhead lodged the complaint in early September, resting it on a report by historian Hans Fässler arguing that between 1719 and 1839 the three cantons invested in and profited from colonial slave-trading structures — Zurich and Bern through stakes in Britain's South Sea Company and Danish colonial bonds, Solothurn through France's Mississippi Company. He demands a criminal investigation, a five-million-franc fine per canton, and personal damages. SRF's assessment is that the move is politically resonant but legally a dead end: slavery is now treated as a crime against humanity, but pinning present-day criminal liability on cantons for 18th-century investments is not a realistic prospect. (SRF, 14.09.2026)

stories.headline: PM-backed candidate wins Okinawa vote
stories.summary: A candidate backed by Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party won Sunday's Okinawa gubernatorial election, unseating the anti-base incumbent who had opposed the US military build-up on the island for more than a decade. Genta Koja, a former deputy mayor of the prefectural capital Naha and backed by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's LDP, took 59% of the vote to defeat two-term governor Denny Tamaki, officials announced on Monday. Tamaki had been a leading voice against the expansion of US bases, including the contested relocation of Marine Corps facilities.
stories.why: the result eases a long-running source of friction between Tokyo and Okinawa over hosting the bulk of US forces in Japan, at a moment when Tokyo is leaning harder on the alliance. (Al Jazeera, 14.09.2026)

stories.headline: Houthis strike Saudi base as Trump stays out
stories.summary: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels claimed a drone-and-missile attack on a military base in southern Saudi Arabia on Sunday 13 September, calling it retaliation for repeated Saudi air raids in Yemen. The group's military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said the strike hit "weapons depots and command-and-control centres" at the Sharurah base, near the Yemeni border. It follows the Houthis' rapid advance this week along Yemen's Red Sea coast, where they consolidated control of the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait — the chokepoint at the southern mouth of the Red Sea — and closed it to Saudi tankers, the story that led yesterday's edition. Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's internationally recognised government against the pro-Iranian fighters, preventively shut down a pipeline after the attacks, Swiss broadcaster SRF reported. Notably, US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he would not intervene militarily: the US outlet Axios reported that de-facto Saudi ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had telephoned Trump twice on Thursday to ask him to strike the Houthis, and Trump said the Houthis had asked him to stay out of the war — a claim relayed on his own account, not independently confirmed. The UN migration agency (IOM) says more than 70,000 people have fled the fighting in western Yemen since the start of September.
stories.why: with Iran already blockading the Strait of Hormuz (the Gulf's main oil chokepoint) for six months, the Houthi gains put Saudi Arabia at risk of losing its maritime outlets for oil at both ends of the peninsula — and Washington's public refusal to defend a core Gulf ally marks a notable shift in US posture.

stories.headline: Russia's record drone barrage spills into Romania
stories.summary: Russia launched one of its largest aerial barrages of the war overnight into Sunday 13 September — 453 attack drones and missiles, of which Ukraine said it destroyed or neutralised 405 drones and four missiles — and a Russian drone crossed into NATO member Romania, which scrambled two F-16 fighter jets. Romania's defence ministry said (in a communiqué reported by Le Monde) that the drone traversed Ukrainian and Moldovan airspace before heading toward the country's north-east; the jets took off from Borcea air base, a public alert was issued in Botoșani county, and forces later found a crashed flying object in a maize field near Botoșenița Mare, in neighbouring Suceava. Separately, the locomotive of a Kyiv–Warsaw passenger train was struck by a Russian drone in Volhynia, north-western Ukraine, about 2 km from the Polish border, the national railway Ukrzaliznytsia said via the Ukrinform agency; passengers were unhurt. Russian strikes on Odesa injured 20 people, and drone attacks killed at least two in the Zhytomyr region and one in Kherson. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said "the Russian barbarians are at your gates" and urged EU and NATO allies to "act now"; President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had fired roughly 2,100 long-range attack drones over the past week.
stories.why: repeated drone incursions into Romanian and Moldovan airspace, and a strike this close to the Polish frontier, keep widening the war's spillover risk onto NATO and EU territory.

stories.headline: Indonesian ferry missing in Java Sea storm
stories.summary: An Indonesian passenger ferry carrying more than 240 people, the Virgo Transport 8, lost contact in bad weather in the Java Sea early on Sunday 13 September, and rescuers were searching for about 140 people after 103 had been evacuated. The vessel had sailed on Saturday from Surabaya, in East Java, toward South Kalimantan on Borneo when it lost contact at around 2 a.m., Indonesia's search-and-rescue agency (Basarnas) said; its Banjarmasin office received a distress report about two hours later and dispatched ships, a rescue team and a helicopter to the ship's last known position. Reuters reported that one person had died among those evacuated, while SRF later put the toll at six as the search continued. Indonesia, an archipelago of some 17,000 islands, relies heavily on ferries and suffers frequent, often deadly maritime accidents blamed on overcrowding and weak safety enforcement.

stories.headline: Five people were killed and around 40 injured when a Dutch tour coach crashed in the Engadin valley of canton Graubünden on Thursday 10 September
stories.summary: at about 4:45 p.m., hitting a guardrail on the road between Susch and Zernez and overturning. The cantonal prosecutor says the cause is not yet established; it is one of the deadliest coach accidents on Swiss roads in years. SRF, 11 Sep 2026

stories.headline: Houthis seize Bab al-Mandab strait
stories.summary: Iran-allied Houthi forces seized control of the Bab al-Mandab strait — the chokepoint at the southern mouth of the Red Sea — closing the route to Saudi tankers, after capturing the port of Mocha on Thursday 10 September and the strategic island of Perim (Mayoun) on Friday 11 September. Perim splits the strait into two narrow shipping channels at its tightest point and carries its own airstrip, so holding it lets the Houthis command the waterway with coastal artillery rather than the missiles and drones they had relied on. In a statement the group said "maritime navigation is safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels," vowing to strike Saudi targets until "the aggression stops and the blockade against our dear people is lifted." Le Monde called it Saudi Arabia's worst military setback in a decade: with Iran having blockaded the Strait of Hormuz (the Gulf's oil chokepoint) off the kingdom's eastern coast for six months, and the Houthis having bombed the pipeline that carries Saudi crude to the Red Sea on Friday, Riyadh risks losing every maritime outlet for its oil and is now seeking direct US support. Bab al-Mandab normally carries roughly a tenth of world seaborne trade and several million barrels of oil a day.
stories.why: two of the three exits for Gulf energy are now contested at once, a step-change in the Iran–Saudi confrontation that threatens global shipping and oil prices well beyond the region.

stories.headline: AI-assisted proofs of fluid blowup
stories.summary: The week's biggest science story needs its framing handled carefully, because the popular version ("AI solved a Millennium Prize problem") is not quite what happened. Here is the accurate version. The Navier–Stokes global-regularity problem — whether smooth fluid flows can spontaneously develop a singularity, a point where the flow is driven infinitely fast in finite time — is one of the six remaining Clay Millennium Prize Problems, each worth $1 million. This week two efforts converged on the surrounding territory. Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster proved finite-time blowup with a smooth forcing term (a mathematically well-behaved external push) for three simpler model systems — the incompressible porous-medium equation, the 2D Boussinesq equations, and the 3D incompressible Euler equations — extending a hand-built strategy due to Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa, and formalising the arguments in Lean (a proof assistant that mechanically checks each logical step). Separately, OpenAI announced that a swarm of autonomous agents had constructed a Lean-checked proof of blowup for Navier–Stokes itself with smooth forcing — a claim that is not peer-reviewed and is entangled in a priority dispute (OpenAI cedes the 3D Euler result to Buckmaster and Alpöge; Buckmaster has suggested the agents may have benefited from his group's work). Tao, who spoke with Buckmaster and is digesting the papers, is explicit that the models do "not quite achieve" the Navier–Stokes goal yet, though the method "has a high likelihood of also extending" to it.
stories.why: it is, by a wide margin, the most consequential mathematical work AI systems have materially contributed to — a real result at the research frontier, not a benchmark score, and machine-checked in Lean so the logic is not in doubt. The cautionary half is the credit-and-verification tangle: as AI produces more mathematics, who did it and what it means are becoming the hard parts, not whether the steps check out. (Read soberly: blowup is an idealised-math statement; real fluids are made of molecules, so nothing here changes how water flows down a drain.) The OpenAI-specific Navier–Stokes claim rests on the company's own announcement, which the sandbox cannot fetch — treat it as an unverified vendor account pending peer review; the Alpöge–Buckmaster results are sourced to Tao's own account.

stories.headline: Redistribution keeps uncensored models alive
stories.summary: A growing set of actors removes built-in refusals from open-weight models ("uncensored" models) and re-uploads them. Rather than argue about it, the authors measure it: between January 2024 and March 2026 they identified 3,471 original uncensored models on Hugging Face, each repackaged an average of 2.4 times, with just three actors accounting for 52% of all 8,164 compressed redistributions. Once a model is quantized (shrunk for easier deployment) and mirrored across separate accounts, formats and registries like Ollama, it persists regardless of whether the original is taken down. Of 1,643 GitHub applications built on these models, they classified 25% as explicitly malicious.
stories.why: it quantifies why "just remove the model" fails as a safety lever — redistribution is the persistence layer, and takedown at the source leaves the mirrors untouched. Concrete numbers are a genuine contribution to the open-weights governance debate, which mostly runs on assertion.

stories.headline: Layer dropout lowers loss when tuned right
stories.summary: Layer dropout (a.k.a. stochastic depth — randomly skipping whole layers during training) once helped transformers train faster and tolerate later pruning, but it quietly vanished from large-model recipes on scattered reports that it hurt accuracy — with, the authors note, no comprehensive study to back the abandonment. They run the missing one: across more than 2,400 training experiments spanning models from 271M to 8.2B parameters and datasets up to 160B tokens, they show that with the right per-layer dropout schedule, timing and optimizer settings, models reach lower loss at the same training FLOPs (a compute-cost measure), or match a target loss while saving up to 25% of training compute. It also unlocks post-training tricks — early exit, layer-skipping, self-speculative decoding — for up to 1.5× inference speedup at negligible accuracy cost.
stories.why: if it holds at frontier scale, this is close to a free efficiency win — the same compute buying a better model, plus cheaper inference — and it is a pointed reminder that the field abandons techniques on folklore as readily as it adopts them. The claim is a reversal of current practice, so independent replication above 8B parameters is the thing to watch.

stories.headline: Verifier soundness caps RL, not compute
stories.summary: This is the cleanest statement yet of where reinforcement-learning-on-reasoning actually has headroom. The authors argue the field's binding constraint is the verification gap: outside formal domains (maths, code) there is no scalable, incorruptible reward. They make it quantitative. In a best-of-N setup (generate N candidate answers, keep the one the verifier rates highest), they show the correlation ρ between verifier and ground truth is an exact "exchange rate" between test-time compute and real capability — and an unsound verifier pays a polynomial penalty as you scale N (roughly N^(1/ρ²)). In program-synthesis tests with executable ground truth, a weak verifier's soundness collapses under optimisation pressure (0.94 → 0.32 at N=4096): selection alone manufactures apparent quality that is really reward hacking (the model gaming the metric rather than improving). Under real GRPO training (a common RL method), a frozen reward model traces the full over-optimisation curve — executed reward collapses 90% — while the same model periodically re-anchored to a 10% stream of real outcomes preserves six times the executed reward.
stories.why: it reframes the whole "just add more inference compute" narrative. Past the domains with a clean checker, more compute against a shaky reward can actively make a model worse, and this paper gives you a way to measure how sound your reward is before you trust the number on top of it.

stories.headline: 122B coding agent trained in a real shell
stories.summary: The most complete public recipe this cycle for training a long-horizon coding agent with RL rather than prompting a closed model. T1 is a 122-billion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model (MoE — only a fraction of the network's "expert" sub-modules fire per token, so it runs far cheaper than its size suggests) trained while operating an actual shell in a cloud sandbox for 300-plus tool-call turns per task, rewarded by executing each task's own test suite. Most of the paper's substance is in stabilising that training: a dense process reward that scores a trajectory by how many verifiers pass, plus two engineering fixes (they call them TITO and R3) that keep the tokens the model trained on aligned with the ones it actually sampled, cutting the train-versus-inference log-probability gap from 0.021 to 0.013. Training tasks were kept deliberately disjoint from the benchmark to guard against memorisation; on Terminal-Bench 2.1 the pipeline lifts the base model from 43.8% to 64.0% of tasks resolved, and on Long-Horizon Terminal-Bench T1 reaches 27.9%, above the reported GPT-5.4 and GLM-5.1.
stories.why: "do real work in a terminal over hundreds of steps" is exactly the coding-assistant frontier, and closing most of the gap to frontier models with an open recipe — one you can inspect and reproduce — is more useful to the field than another closed benchmark score. It is also a concrete demonstration of thread #1: the reward here is sound (the tests either pass or they don't), which is precisely why it works.

stories.headline: Running a skill as a subagent beats pasting it
stories.summary: "Agent skills" are reusable capability bundles — instructions, scripts, resources — that an agent normally uses by loading the instructions into its own context window and following them. The paper tests the alternative: invoke the skill as a subagent with a fresh context window instead. As task horizons grow, loading everything into one context becomes brittle because reasoning quality degrades as the context fills; subagent execution avoids that by handing each subtask a clean slate. The finding is refreshingly specific: subagents win when a skill exposes a clear input→output contract and its instructions genuinely encode the procedure to fulfil it. The cost is coordination overhead — extra tokens spent talking between the main agent and its subagents.
stories.why: this is a live architecture decision for anyone building on agent frameworks today (it is exactly the subagents-versus-skills question in tools like Claude Code), and the paper names the precise condition — a clean contract — under which delegation pays for its overhead rather than just burning tokens.

stories.headline: Why post-training quantization barely hurts
stories.summary: Post-training quantization stores a trained model's weights at lower precision (e.g. 4-bit) to shrink it, and each rounded weight injects a small error into the model's hidden states. Naively those errors should compound layer by layer and wreck predictions — and in a randomly initialised network they do. So why don't they in a pretrained one, which was never trained to tolerate the noise? The authors find two mechanisms that emerge during pretraining. First, the error a layer newly introduces tends to oppose the error it inherited from below, so the two partially cancel and the full-precision-versus-quantized discrepancy grows slowly. Second, the output ("LM-head") geometry preferentially preserves the scores and probabilities of the top, most-confident tokens.
stories.why: quantization is how large models fit on modest or local hardware, and it has largely been an empirical dark art. A mechanistic account of why it survives also tells you where it should break — long reasoning chains and low-confidence token predictions, where the cancellation has more chances to fail — turning a trial-and-error craft into something you can reason about.

stories.headline: Manufacturing rewards for tasks with no answer key
stories.summary: RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR — training against an automatic correctness check) works for maths and code but not for diagnosis, where establishing the true cause of an anomaly needs costly expert investigation and may stay ambiguous even afterward. TRACE sidesteps the asymmetry by engineering it away: it samples a hidden intervention, injects it into a controlled simulator, and generates the observations that intervention would produce — so the injected cause is the ground-truth label and gives an objective reward, while the agent still has to investigate noisy, confounded evidence using Python and SQL. In a digital-advertising diagnostic environment with 12 root causes, supervised fine-tuning lifts a 35B model from 0.159 to 0.637 full-attribution accuracy, and subsequent RL reaches 0.757 — above every prompted baseline tested, including Claude Opus 5 at 0.686 and a prompted 122B model — while using substantially fewer tool calls.
stories.why: it is a general trick for extending RLVR into domains where verification is normally expensive — synthesise the world so the answer is known by construction — and it shows a mid-size open model overtaking frontier closed models on the resulting task. Read together with Proof-Carrying Cognition, the two papers are the same coin: one measures the cost of an unsound reward, the other builds a sound one where none existed.

stories.headline: BRICS summit opens in New Delhi
stories.summary: The annual BRICS summit — the bloc of major non-Western economies, now marking its 20th year — formally opened in New Delhi on Saturday 12 September, with China's Xi Jinping arriving in India for the first time in seven years to join Russia's Vladimir Putin and Iran's Masoud Pezeshkian. Host Narendra Modi held talks on Friday with Putin (agreeing to deepen ties) and with Pezeshkian (raising freedom of navigation and the safety of ship crews). Also attending are Egypt's Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, Ethiopia's Abiy Ahmed and Indonesia's Prabowo Subianto, plus the WHO and WTO chiefs and UN Secretary-General António Guterres; Brazil's Lula sent his foreign minister. The agenda is dominated by the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine disrupting energy and shipping, US tariffs — President Trump has branded the bloc "anti-American" and threatened punitive levies on members — and expanding non-Western cross-border payment channels.
stories.why: the Xi–Modi thaw and the choreography of Putin and Pezeshkian in New Delhi is a visible bid by the "Global South" to coordinate against Washington's tariff pressure, though the bloc's own divisions (a May foreign-ministers' meeting ended with no joint statement on Iran) limit how far it can go.

stories.headline: France train derailment probed as sabotage
stories.summary: A regional TER (French inter-city train) running from Rouen to Caen derailed near Cléon in Normandy at about 19:45 on Friday 11 September, injuring 44 of the 186 people aboard. An 18-year-old woman was evacuated by helicopter in critical condition and the other 43 were treated for lesser injuries; 130 firefighters, five medical teams and 80 vehicles responded. Investigators are now treating deliberate sabotage as the main line of inquiry after a severed rail fragment was found on the track, according to police sources; the Rouen prosecutor said on Friday night that the cause was not yet established, that the driver's alcohol and drug tests were negative, and that "the investigation will be long."
stories.why: if sabotage is confirmed it would be a deliberate attack on France's passenger rail network; for now the malicious-act hypothesis is the lead line, not a finding.

stories.headline: OpenAI opens its Agents API
stories.summary: OpenAI opens its Agents API — the plumbing behind Codex and ChatGPT. Now in public beta, it lets developers build cloud agents that run for hours, execute code and process files on the same infrastructure that powers Codex and ChatGPT, with automatic context management, parallel tool use, and delegation to sub-agents. Developers can use OpenAI-hosted sandboxes or partners (Cloudflare, Vercel, Oracle); OpenAI says there are no extra fees beyond token usage, and it builds on the open-source Codex harness with MCP and custom-function support.

stories.headline: Fable 5.1 edges Astra on ErdosBench
stories.summary: On research-grade maths, Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra finish in a near dead heat. ErdosBench scores models on 226 Erdős-inspired open maths problems, graded not by raw solve-count but by an external judge on an A–F scale (A = sound and appropriately scoped; C = a material gap; D/F = misleading or contradicted), with model-specific proof audits — a deliberately harder-to-game signal than "problems solved." On the full run, Fable 5.1 (xhigh) leads with a 3.25 judge average (grade mix A=104 / B=112 / C=10, no D/F), edging GPT-6 Astra (xhigh) at 3.23 (A=106 / B=102 / C=18) by 0.024 points — the leaderboard calls it an audit-level tie, with Fable stronger at conservatively-scoped partial work and Astra the better "theorem closer." Both sit well short of saturation: this is a real but modest step on research-math reasoning, not a solved benchmark, and it lands the same week OpenAI moved GPT-6 Astra to general release.

stories.headline: US names six Chinese AI distillers
stories.summary: US agencies name six Chinese firms over "industrial-scale" model distillation. In a joint release on Tuesday 2026-09-08, the NSA, CISA and FBI alleged that DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, MiniMax, StepFun and Z.AI have run large-scale efforts since at least late 2024 to distil the capabilities of US frontier models — including variants of Claude, GPT, Gemini and Grok — "likely" with "Chinese government awareness." Distillation here means training a model on another model's outputs to copy its behaviour cheaply. Read this as a government allegation, not an adjudicated finding: it is the agencies' characterisation, the named firms have not been shown to have responded, and "likely" and "awareness" are doing load-bearing work in the claim.

stories.headline: Vaud PLR renews its three ministers
stories.summary: The PLR Vaud (the canton's liberal-radical party) endorsed its three sitting cantonal ministers — Christelle Luisier, Isabelle Moret and Frédéric Borloz — for re-election, at a party congress in Yvonand on Thursday 10 September. The trio, the party's only declared candidates, were confirmed by acclamation and will run for the Conseil d'État (Vaud's seven-member cantonal executive) at the February–March 2027 election as part of the centre-right "Alliance vaudoise," alongside Jean-François Thuillard of the UDC (Union démocratique du centre — the right-wing Swiss People's Party). The move locks in the incumbent centre-right slate roughly six months before the vote.

stories.headline: Algeria severs ties with the UAE
stories.summary: Algeria severed diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates on Thursday 10 September, citing "provocative and hostile acts," and said it would begin closing its airspace to the UAE from Friday. Algiers gave the Emirati ambassador 48 hours and said it acted "after exhausting all avenues," though commercial flights to and from Algiers may continue until the end of 2026. Relations have been strained for years over what Algeria calls the UAE's expanding influence in North and West Africa; Algiers has accused Abu Dhabi of working to destabilise Libya, Mali and Sudan — including backing the Rapid Support Forces (RSF, a Sudanese paramilitary) in that country's civil war, a charge the UAE denies. The UAE said it hoped the decision would prove "temporary."

stories.headline: Putin joins BRICS summit in New Delhi
stories.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in New Delhi on Friday 11 September for a summit of the BRICS bloc (Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa and newer members — the group of major emerging economies), with talks alongside Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian and India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi expected the same day. Le Temps reports the gathering convenes amid strains on the bloc's cohesion, from the conflict in the Middle East to the war in Ukraine.

stories.headline: EU committee backs Swiss Bilaterals III
stories.summary: The European Parliament's foreign affairs committee (AFET) approved the Switzerland–EU "Bilaterals III" package on Thursday 10 September by 53 votes to 3. a lopsided endorsement on the EU side of a treaty that has yet to clear either parliament's plenary. Christophe Grudler, the French Renew MEP who is the file's rapporteur, called the vote an "étape importante" (important step) and said Brussels has no "plan B" if the deal fails. It follows the Swiss Council of States' committees, which on 4 September advanced the package on the domestic side but insisted it must pass a double majority of voters and cantons — so the ratification road still runs through a Swiss popular vote.
stories.why: Bilaterals III governs free movement, the single market and research access that directly shape how people in Switzerland live, work and study with the EU; a strong committee signal in Brussels narrows the question to whether Swiss voters will ratify.

stories.headline: Federal Council upholds 'Lex On'
stories.summary: The Federal Council has come out in favour of keeping the so-called "Lex On," recommending that parliament reject two motions that sought to undo a March amendment to the Swissness law. The change lets companies add the Swiss cross to labels such as "Swiss engineering" or "Swiss design" under certain conditions even when the product itself is made abroad — the Zurich brand On, whose shoes are manufactured in Asia, is the emblematic case. The government says it will accompany the looser practice with an "evaluation of the Swissness provisions." The two reversal motions came from PLR politician Daniela Schneeberger and Centre politician Fabio Regazzi; industrial circles, including in Vaud, have called the loosening a "dilution" of a "fabulous" asset and, in the sharpest framing, a "trahison" (betrayal) of firms that actually produce in Switzerland.
stories.why: the Swiss cross is a paid-for marketing premium, and who may use it — genuine domestic manufacturers or brands that design here but build elsewhere — is a direct commercial fight over the value of "made in Switzerland."

stories.headline: Explosion kills two at Ritom plant
stories.summary: Two workers were killed in an explosion at the Ritom hydroelectric plant in Piotta, in Italian-speaking Ticino, shortly after 9:30 am on Wednesday 9 September. Ticino cantonal police, who described it as a "serious workplace accident," said a fire broke out inside the building and that, on a preliminary reconstruction, an explosion involving two workers left both dead of their injuries; one was a 55-year-old Swiss national and the other was still being formally identified. The 1917-era plant was undergoing a renovation in which new electrical machinery had recently been installed in the old section where the blast occurred. The cause remains under investigation.

stories.headline: US strikes Iranian tankers; Iran hits Jordan base
stories.summary: The United States struck five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday 8 September, and Iran retaliated overnight by firing some 20 ballistic missiles at a US military base in Jordan — 18 of which Jordan's air force said it intercepted early Wednesday 9 September. [ongoing since 2026-09-05]. US Central Command (CENTCOM — the US military's Middle East headquarters) said it hit four tankers in the Gulf of Oman (the Kaviz, Charminar, Horizon 1 and Riesco) and one, the Derya, near Kharg Island off the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow Gulf chokepoint through which roughly a fifth of the world's seaborne oil passes — after the IRGC (Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, Iran's elite military branch) twice targeted a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles. CENTCOM said crews were ordered to abandon ship beforehand and reported no casualties, and cast the vessels as a "multibillion-dollar shadow network" funding Iran's proxies — its own characterisation, not an independently verified finding. Jordan, a US ally that hosts an American base, said 20 missiles were fired toward its territory and two fell in unpopulated areas; a US official called the strike ineffective, with all personnel accounted for. The IRGC said it hit two US ships, eight tankers and 10 other "non-compliant" vessels in the Strait, and warned tankers off Bahrain and Kuwait to leave or be targeted; oil rose above $100 a barrel for the first time in nearly six weeks.
stories.why: the first Iranian missile strike on Jordanian soil widens a naval war that had been largely confined to the Gulf's shipping lanes, and the threat to tankers off Kuwait and Bahrain — with crude back over $100 — signals the disruption is spreading from Iran's own exports toward the wider Gulf supply that Europe partly depends on.

stories.headline: AI agents claim a Navier-Stokes blowup
stories.summary: On Tuesday 8 September, OpenAI announced that a swarm of roughly 10,000 autonomous AI agents — running on an internal model not released to the public — had constructed a proof that the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations can develop a singularity (a "blowup," where some infinitesimal patch of fluid is driven to flow infinitely fast in finite time). The Navier–Stokes equations apply Newton's second law to fluids, and whether their smooth solutions can blow up is one of the six remaining Millennium Prize Problems posed by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000, each worth $1 million. OpenAI says its result is the version with a smooth forcing term (a mathematically well-behaved external push) and finite energy throughout — a legitimate form of the problem — and that the whole argument was formally checked in Lean, a proof-assistant language that mechanically verifies each logical step. By the company's account the agents worked about 88 hours, exchanged ~2.7 million messages, and burned ~130 billion output tokens at a cost of several million dollars (per OpenAI's Sébastien Bubeck). The result has not been peer-reviewed, and even a Lean-verified proof leaves open what it means: mathematicians will need time to judge whether it truly settles the prize's specific formulation. Independently, twelve hours earlier, Tristan Buckmaster (NYU) and Levent Alpöge (Anthropic) had announced finite-time blowup with smooth forcing for three related systems — incompressible porous-media flow, the Boussinesq equations, and 3D incompressible Euler — also with a Lean formalization, after nearly a year of work using Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's Codex. Both efforts lean heavily on a strategy developed by Diego Córdoba (ICMAT, Madrid) and Luis Martínez-Zoroa (CUNEF, Madrid); Charles Fefferman of Princeton, who wrote the Clay problem's official statement, called those two "the heroes of the story." The dispute is twofold: OpenAI cedes priority on the 3D Euler result to Buckmaster and Alpöge but claims Navier–Stokes for itself, while Buckmaster has suggested OpenAI's researchers or agents may have benefited from his group's work through their own models — and, separately, the mathematical significance is still being weighed even though the code checks out. As reported by Quanta, timelines and credit remain unsettled.
stories.why: If it holds, it is by a wide margin the most consequential mathematical proof an AI system has produced — a real result on a century-and-a-half-old question about turbulence, not a benchmark score. But the credit tangle is the cautionary half of the story: the decisive ideas came from two European mathematicians working by hand, and "an AI proved it" flattens a messier, more human picture. (Read soberly: the blowup is an idealized-math statement — real fluids are made of molecules, so nothing here changes how water flows down a drain.)
